div.p: Ordinal data such as Likert items, ratings, or generic ordered variables are widespread in psychology. These variables are usually analyzed using metric models (e.g., standard linear regression) with important drawbacks in terms of statistical inference (reduced power and increased type-1 error) and prediction. One possible reason for not using ordinal regression models could be difficulty in understanding parameters or conducting a power analysis.
The tutorial aims to present ordinal regression models using a simulation-based approach.
Firstly, we introduced the general model highlighting crucial components and assumptions.

Then, we explained how to interpret parameters for a logit and probit model. Then we proposed two ways for simulating data as a function of predictors showing a 2x2 interaction with categorical predictors and the interaction between a numeric and categorical predictor.

Finally, we showed an example of power analysis using simulations that can be easily extended to complex models with multiple predictors. The tutorial is supported by a collection of custom R functions developed to simulate and understand ordinal regression models. The code to reproduce the proposed simulation, the custom R functions, and additional examples of ordinal regression models can be found on the online Open Science Framework repository (https://osf.io/93h5j).

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Psychological research makes extensive use of ordinal data. One of the main reasons is probably the usage of Likert scales (Likert, 1932). Ordinal data, as defined by Stevens (1946), belongs to a specific type of measurement scale where ordered numbers are assigned to a variable. Beyond Likert-like items, there are several applications of ordinal scales in Psychology. For instance, sociodemographic variables like educational levels or socioeconomic status, as well as general ratings such as pain severity, agreement with a statement, or the evaluation of sensory experiences (e.g., Overgaard & Sandberg, 2021).

In contrast to nominal scales, the labels in ordinal scales are ordered. Unlike interval or ratio scales, there is no explicit assumption about the distance between labels. An example is asking people the degree of agreement about a certain statement using a scale from 1 (no agreement) to 7 (total agreement). Answering 4 compared to 2 suggests a higher agreement but we cannot affirm that there is two times the agreement compared to the second answer. Stevens (1946) and Kemp and Grace (2021) suggested that for ordinal variables it is appropriate to calculate ranks-based descriptive statistics (e.g., median or percentiles) instead of metric statistics (e.g., mean or standard deviation) and use appropriate inferential tools (Agresti, 2010;e.g., Cliff, 1996). This distinction in terms of the appropriateness of certain descriptive statistics is also relevant when modeling data.
Treating ordinal data as metric refers to assuming the labels as actual integer numbers, thus assuming a fixed and known distance between levels (Liddell & Kruschke, 2018).

In Psychology, especially with item-based measures (questionnaires, surveys, etc.), the common practice is running a linear regression that makes an explicit assumption about metric features of the response variable. Liddell and Kruschke (2018) reviewed the psychological literature using Likert-based measures and reported how the majority of papers used metric-based statistical models. In the same work, Liddell and Kruschke (2018) showed examples of the potential pitfalls of metric models applied to ordinal variables (but see Robitzsch, 2020 for an alternative perspective for factor analysis). They reported problems in terms of lack of power, inversion of the effects (e.g., finding a negative effect when the true effect is positive), biased estimates, and increased type-1 error. One of the main reasons is that the metric model assumes normality of the response variable, while ordinal data are discrete and often highly skewed, bounded, and multimodal. While sums or averages of ordinal items could be treated as metric (Carifio & Perla, 2008;Carifio & Perla, 2007; but see Jamieson, 2004) Liddell and Kruschke (2018) provided some examples of potential pitfalls even in this case. In the current paper, we discuss only cases where there is a single ordinal outcome (e.g., a single item, question, etc.) without considering the case of aggregating ordinal responses. Beyond the regression models presented in the tutorial, ordinal regression models are also relevant for psychometric modeling. Li (2016) showed that confirmatory factor analysis conducted using ordinal models produced less biased estimations compared to using a metric model. Ordinal models are also widely used in Item Response Theory (IRT) with polytomous items (e.g., Dai et al., 2021) Despite the extensive usage of Likert scales in Psychology there is a lack of introductory papers about ordinal regression models. Bürkner and Vuorre (2019) provided an introductory tutorial on fitting Bayesian ordinal regressions while Liddell and Kruschke (2018) provided a more advanced comparison with standard linear regression.

The current paper proposed a simulation-based approach (e.g., DeBruine & Barr, 2021) for understanding the model and estimating the statistical power. For the tutorial, we assume that the reader is familiar with basic R programming and introductory theory about linear regression. Similar to other tutorials (DeBruine & Barr, 2021;Gambarota & Altoè, 2024) we used a few equations that are necessary to understand the model parameters and implement the Monte Carlo simulation.

In the first part, we introduce the ordinal models explaining the general structure and assumptions. Then we move with model fitting and parameters interpretation. Finally, we introduce the simulation approach for common research scenarios and an application to power analysis. We used R [Version 4.4.1; R Core Team (2024)] for the code, figures, and tables. The tutorial is supported by a set of custom R functions that can be found on the online OSF repository (https://osf.io/93h5j) and the related GitHub repository https://GitHub.com/shared-research/ordinalsim. In the GitHub repository, the README file contains overall information about loading and using the custom functions.
For the tutorial, we used the following packages.

div.head: Ordinal regression models
div.p: We can generally define ordinal regression, as a statistical model explicitly considering the ordinal (and not metric) nature of the response variable. The nomenclature of ordinal regression models can be confusing but Tutz (2022) and Bürkner and Vuorre (2019) provide a clear and updated taxonomy of ordinal regression models.

We can identify three main models: cumulative models (CM, Agresti, 2010;McCullagh, 1980), sequential models (Tutz, 1990), and adjacent category models. Among these, the CM is the most widely used, assuming the existence of a latent variable categorized using a set of thresholds. The sequential model is appropriate when modeling sequential processes where responding to a certain category implies having already reached lower categories. The adjacent category model compares a category with the next one and can be seen the adjacent-category model can be seen as a series of binomial regressions taking into account the ordering (Tutz, 2022).

In the current paper, we focus on the CM for several reasons. Firstly, the latent formulation of the model is particularly convenient for parameter interpretation and data simulation. The second reason is that several psychological constructs can be formalized as a latent continuous variable observed as an ordinal item(s). Furthermore, the signal detection theory framework that is very common in experimental psychology can be implemented using a CM (e.g., DeCarlo, 2010). Figure 1 depicts the overall structure of the CM.

div.head: Model notation
div.p: In this section, we introduce some notations for the CM to be consistent with the existing literature (e.g., Agresti, 2010) and the ordinal R package. We define 𝑌 𝑘 as the observed ordinal variable with 𝑘 levels and 𝑌 ⋆ is the underlying latent variable. The latent variable is segmented using 𝑘 -1 thresholds 𝛼 1 , … , 𝛼 𝑘-1 . Similarly to the generalized linear model framework (e.g., Fox, 2015), we define 𝑔(𝑝) = 𝜂 as the link function that maps probabilities into the linear predictor 𝜂. To transform back 𝜂 into probabilities we use the inverse of the link function 𝑝 = 𝑔 -1 (𝜂). The specific link function defines the type of model and requires different R functions. For example, using a Normal distribution (probit link function) requires using the cumulative distribution function 𝑔(𝑝) = Φ -1 (𝑝) = 𝜂 and the inverse of the link function is the inverse cumulative distribution function (or quantile function) defined 𝑝 = 𝑔 -1 (𝜂) = Φ(𝜂).

When modeling an ordinal variable in a CM we include predictors on the cumulative probability 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 𝑘), 𝑘 = 1, … , 𝑘 -1 1 . Equation (1) shows the general cumulative model with model matrix X and the vector of coefficients 𝛽 . The minus sign it is used to interpret the 𝛽 𝑗 as in the standard regression models where higher positive values correspond to an increased probability of responding to higher 𝑘 categories (Agresti, 2010).

The 𝛽 ⊤ x 𝑖 is the linear predictor 𝜂 𝑖 that is the cumulative probability 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 𝑘) transformed using the link function 𝑔(⋅). The probability of a single outcome 𝑃 (𝑌 = 𝑘) can be calculated as the difference between cumulative probabilities (see Equation ( 2)).

div.p: There are always two special cases when computing the probability of a single outcome 𝑌 that is when 𝑌 = 1 and 𝑌 = 𝑘. In the first case the cumulative probability is calculated from -∞ (assuming that 𝛼 0 = -∞). In the second case (𝑌 = 𝑘) the probability is calculated as 𝑃 (𝑌 𝑖 = 𝑘) = 1 -𝑔 -1 (𝛼 𝑘-1 -𝛽 ⊤ x 𝑖 ) (assuming that 𝛼 𝑘 = +∞). div.p: The 𝜖 term is the random part (errors) of the model. For a probit model, errors are distributed as a standard Normal distribution, and for a logit model as a standard logistic distribution. Following the notation by Tutz (2022), the observed ordinal value 𝑌 𝑖 = 𝑘 comes from 𝑌 ⋆ 𝑖 belonging to the interval defined by the thresholds 𝑌 𝑖 = 𝑘 ⟺ 𝛼 𝑘-1 < 𝑌 ⋆ 𝑖 < 𝛼 𝑘 where -∞ = 𝛼 0 < 𝛼 1 < ⋯ < 𝛼 𝑘-1 < 𝛼 𝑘 = ∞.

In the CM, thresholds 𝛼 𝑘 are considered fixed and part of the measurement procedure (Liddell & Kruschke, 2018; but see the location-shift models by Tutz, 2022, where thresholds vary as a function of predictors) and can be considered as intercepts. The proposed CM can be parametrized in different ways. Liddell and Kruschke (2018) proposed a Bayesian version of the model and Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari (2020) proposed other threshold parametrizations.

div.head: Link function
div.p: The CM implemented in Equations ( 1) and (3) requires specifying the link function 𝑔(⋅) or the errors distribution 𝜖 𝑖 ∼ 𝐷(0, 𝜎) (𝐷 being a certain probability distribution with 𝜎 being the scale of the distribution ). Among several available functions, the logit and probit models are the most common. The logit model uses a logit link function and a standard logistic distribution as a latent variable. On the other side, the probit model assumes a standard Normal distribution using the inverse of the cumulative distribution (Φ -1 (⋅)) function as the link function.

Although the two models provide similar results, the main difference lies in the parameter interpretation, which stems from the different assumed distributions for the error term. The logit link is often chosen because it is the canonical link function and is the default in many R packages and functions for fitting these models. Furthermore, interpreting effects as odds ratios (estimated via logit models) can usually be more intuitive compared to differences in z scores (estimated via probit models). However, when fitting signal detection theory models, the probit model is more appropriate. Another consideration is the underlying assumed process for the dependent variable. If the dependent variable is assumed to be the result of dichotomizing or segmenting a continuous underlying variable, the probit model is more intuitive because it uses a standard normal distribution. In the next sections, we will delve deeper into the differences between logit and probit models and present the associated simulation strategies.

To provide an initial understanding of the basic differences between these models, Figure 2 illustrates the two error term distributions, while Table 1 summarizes the presented CM, the proposed link function, and the corresponding R code.

In terms of parameters, both distributions can be defined in terms of location 𝜇 and scale 𝜎. The standard normal distribution has 𝜇 = 0 and standard deviation 𝜎 = 1. The standard deviation of the logistic distribution is 𝜎𝜋 √ 3 . The standard logistic distribution has 𝜇 = 0 and 𝜎 = 1 thus the standard deviation simplifies to 𝜋 √ 3 ≈ 1.81. In practical terms, fixing 𝜇 and 𝜎 leads to a higher standard deviation for the logistic distribution. In the supplementary materials, we showed how to implement location-scale models for including predictors on the scale parameter (Cox, 1995;Rigby & Stasinopoulos, 2005;Tutz, 2022). div.head: Model fitting
div.p: For fitting the CM we used the ordinal package (Christensen, 2023) that provides a complete and intuitive way to implement the ordinal models. The syntax is very similar to standard linear models in R with functions to calculate predictions, perform model comparison, and, extract relevant model information.foot_0
The main function is clm() and the formula is specified using the syntax y ~...
where y is the ordinal response and ... is a combination of predictors. The package also implements mixed-effects models including random intercepts and slopes.
When fitting the model the crucial arguments are the formula, the link function, and the data. More advanced arguments are nominal, scale, and threshold.
• formula: the formula y ~x with the dependent variable and predictors.
• link: is the link function (in this tutorial only logit and probit)
• data: is the dataset with variables included in the formula
• nominal: formula with predictors where the proportional odds assumption (see the Proportional odds assumption section) is relaxed (i.e., partial or non-proportional odds)
• scale: formula with predictors for the scale parameter for fitting a scale-location model
• threshold: different structures for estimating the thresholds. The default is threshold = "flexible" where 𝑘 -1 thresholds (where 𝑘 is the number of ordinal levels for 𝑌 ) are estimated.

We can start by fitting a simple model, highlighting the crucial parameters where the detailed explanation will be expanded in the next sections. Table 2 contains simulated data from 𝑛 = 100 where participants rated the agreement about an item with 𝑘 = 4 ordered options. The participants are divided into two groups (𝑎 and 𝑏). We can fit a cumulative link model (clm() function) and check the model summary.

div.head: Group Mean Median
div.p: The two main sections of the model summary are the Coefficients section reporting the regression coefficients 𝛽 and the Threshold section reporting the 𝛼 estimation. Given that 𝑘 = 4 we have 𝑘 -1 = 3 thresholds and one 𝛽 associated with the 𝑥 effect. As in standard regression models, when 𝑥 is a categorical predictor with 𝑗 levels, we will estimate 𝑗 -1 regression coefficients (plus the intercept term) where the interpretation depends on the contrast coding (see Schad, Vasishth, Hohenstein, & Kliegl, 2020). In R the default is the dummy coding where a factor of 𝑗 levels is converted into 𝑗 -1 dummy variables. By default, the first level of the factor is taken as the reference level and the 𝑗 -1 coefficients represent the comparison between the other levels and the reference.

div.head: Logit Model. Odds and odds ratio
div.p: To understand the logit model we need to introduce odds and odds ratio. The odds of a probability 𝑝 is defined as 𝑝/(1 -𝑝) thus the success probability over the failure probability. The odds take values ranging from 0 to ∞. With a probability of 𝑝 = 0.8, we have odds of 4, indicating that there are four successes for each failure. The same as having 𝑝 = 0.2 and an odds of 0.25 means that for each 0.25 successes, we have a failure (or 4 failures for each success). When comparing two groups or conditions we can take the ratio of two odds. An odds ratio (OR) of 4 means that the odds of success at the numerator are 4 times higher than the odds of success at the denominator. The logit transformation is about taking the logarithm of the odds creating a symmetric function ranging from -∞ to ∞ with 𝑝 = 0.5 as the midpoint because log(0.5/(1 -0.5)) = 0.

Odds and odds ratios are clearly defined with 𝑘 = 2 outcomes. In fact, a standard logistic regression estimates the log odds ratio between the two groups. With an ordinal variable we have 𝑘 -1 odds ratios determined by the cumulative probability in terms of 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 1), … , 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 𝑘 -1) comparing the two groups.
For example, the probability of responding 𝑌 ≤ 1 in the group "a" is 0.22 corresponding to an odds of 0.28. When calculating the odds ratio comparing "a" vs "b"
for 𝑌 ≤ 1 we obtain that the group "a" has 3.24 times the odds of responding 𝑌 ≤ 1 compared to the group "b". # calculating the cumulative probability for k -1 variables.

div.head: Proportional odds assumption
div.p: The CM estimates the (cumulative) OR as a function of predictors. The 𝑘 -1 ORs are similar to each other (increasing 𝑛 will increase the similarity due to the reduced sampling error) because data are generated under the so-called proportional odds (PO) assumption. In the code below we simulated a large sample size (see the next section for the R code related to the simulation) showing that the estimated ORs are almost the same.

The basic version of the CM model fitted above assumes the PO estimating a single 𝛽 (instead of 𝑘 -1). The PO assumption is formalized in Equation ( 4). The cumulative log odds ratio comparing 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 𝑘|x 0 ) with 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 𝑘|x 1 ) (𝑥 0 and 𝑥 1 being two levels of a predictor) is the same regardless of the specific threshold (𝛽 1 = 𝛽 2 ⋯ = 𝛽 𝑘-1 ). Figure ( 4) depicts the proportional odds assumption for the 𝑘 -1 logistic curves both for probabilities and linear predictors 𝜂. In practical terms, having an ordinal variable from strongly disagree to strongly agree, the effect of the predictors on moving from strongly disagree to disagree is the same as from disagree to neutral.
[Figure 4 about here]

There are CM models relaxing this assumption completely (non proportional odds, Tutz, 2022) or partially (partial proportional odds, Peterson & Harrell, 1990). The advantage of the PO model is the parsimony. In some scenarios, the PO assumption can be considered too strict. There are several methods for testing if data supports the PO (see Liu, He, Tu, & Tang, 2023 for an overview). Tutz and Berger (2020) suggested a trade-off between assuming/relaxing the PO assumption by fitting location-shift or location-scale models. Basically, these methods should guarantee more flexibility in modelling the observed probabilities reducing the number of parameters. However, these methods and models are outside the scope of the tutorial (see the supplementary materials)

The PO can also be seen calculating the ORs using predicted probabilities. By default, the model fitted with clm() assumes the PO. In the following code block, we computed the odds ratio comparing 𝑥 𝑎 and 𝑥 𝑏 when 𝑘 ≤ 1 and 𝑘 ≤ 2.
# fitting the model fit <-clm(y ~x, data = dat, link = "logit")
# extracting the predicted probabilities for the two groups pr <-predict(fit, data.frame(x = unique(dat$x)))$fit
# odds ratio y <= 1 (a vs b) VS y <= 2 (a vs b)

div.head: Probit Model and z scores
div.p: The previous model was fitted using a logit link function. When assuming a standard normal distribution we are fitting probit model. The main difference regards the interpretation of parameters. In the logit model, the regression coefficient is the log odds ratio. For categorical variables they represent the increase in the log odds of moving from one category to another while for numerical variables is the increase in the log odds for a unit increase in the predictor

In the probit model, the regression coefficient is the increase in terms of 𝑧 scores for a unit increase in 𝑥. This is very convenient especially for categorical variables because parameters can be interpreted as a Cohen's 𝑑-like measure. In terms of latent distributions, 𝛽 is the shift in the latent mean (i.e., location) comparing two or more groups or the rate of change of the latent scores with respect 𝑥 . More formally the shift in the latent distribution is 𝛽/𝜎 (for the probit model 𝜎 = 1). The interpretation in terms of shifting the latent mean holds also for the logistic model. However, the standard deviation of the standard logistic regression is 𝜋 √ 3 ≈ 1.81 The 𝛽 for the logistic distribution can be interpreted as the location shift of the latent logistic distribution by 𝛽/( 𝜋 √ 3 ) standard deviations (Agresti, 2010).

Proportional odds and probit model. More generally, the PO assumption can be called parallel slopes assumption. When applying the link function, cumulative probabilities are no longer a sigmoid shape but linear (see Figure 4). When the 𝑘 -1 lines are parallel this means that the 𝑘 -1 slopes are the same. The PO assumption is relevant only for the logit model because the parameters are ORs.

For the probit model, the difference in 𝑧 scores for a unit increase in 𝑥 is the same regardless of the threshold (see Equation ( 5)). As for the previous example, we can fit the CM and manually calculate the difference in 𝑧 scores (from predicted probabilities).

div.head: Simulating data
div.p: In this tutorial, we present two methods for simulating ordinal data. Simulating data is a powerful strategy for understanding the model (DeBruine & Barr, 2021) and estimating statistical properties (e.g., power or type-1 error). The first simulation method calculates the probabilities of each 𝑌 level as a function of predictors and generates data from a multinomial distribution. The second method simulates data using the latent formulation. Whenever random number generation occurs, it is appropriate to set a seed (set.seed() function, in this case, we use set.seed( 2024)). Running again the same code with the same seed will produce the same result.

A general simulation approach concerns generating a dataset from the assumed data generation process, fitting the statistical model, and assessing the recovery of simulated parameters. To check the simulation approach, using a large sample size produce estimations with small sampling errors. A limited sample size even when fitting the true model will produce variable estimations.

Simulating from a multinomial distribution. For the first method, we need to calculate 𝑃 (𝑌 𝑖 ≤ 𝑘) = 𝑔 -1 (𝜂 𝑖 ) as a function of predictors and then sample from a multinomial (more specifically categorical) distribution using the sample() function in R. This method is similar to the general way of simulating data for a generalized linear model (see the supplementary materials).

As a simple example, we simulate two groups with 𝑛 = 100 participants responding to an item (𝑌 ) with 𝑘 = 4 ordered options. As explained in the previous sections, we can summarise the effect size of a CM (assuming PO) using a single 𝛽 = log(𝑂𝑅) = log(3).

The following code summarises the first steps of the simulation. We define the simulation parameters, calculate the 𝑘 -1 thresholds 𝛼, and apply Equations ( 1) and (2) calculating the probability of each response.

To set the thresholds, we can consider them as intercepts thus the transformed probabilities of each ordinal response when 𝑥 = 0 (in this case the first group). The alpha_to_prob() and prob_to_alpha() can be used to go back and forth from thresholds and probabilities. We can generalize the previous workflow as:

1. Define simulation parameters, intercept probabilities 2. Define regression coefficients 𝛽 and calculate the 𝑘 -1 linear predictors (𝜂) using the equations 3. Apply the inverse of the link function 𝑔 -1 (𝜂) on the linear predictor and calculate the cumulative probabilities 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 1|x), 𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 2|x), ...𝑃 (𝑌 ≤ 𝑘 -1|x)
4. Calculate the probabilities of 𝑘 outcomes 5. Sample 𝑛 outcomes from a multinomial distribution using the calculated probabilities 6. Fit the appropriate model using ordinal::clm()

Simulating from the latent distribution. More efficiently, we can use the latent formulation of the CM. This requires simulating a standard linear regression using the appropriate data generation function (logistic or normal) and cutting the latent variable using the thresholds. The workflow is slightly different compared to the previous approach.
1. Define simulation parameters as in the previous simulation. prob0 are the probabilities when all predictors are zero.
2. Define regression coefficients and calculate the linear predictor 𝜂 using the Equation

3. Add the random errors 𝜖 𝑖 sampling from the logistic or normal distributions 4. Cut the latent variable into 𝑘 areas using the thresholds 𝛼 and assign the corresponding ordinal value. This can be done using the cut() or the findInterval() functions. set.seed(2024) N <-100 # sample size or <-4 # odds ratio, higher here just for a more clear plot #> Estimate Std. Error z value #> 1|2 -1.2336 0.3076 -4.010 #> 2|3 -0.1924 0.2667 -0.721 #> 3|4 0.8755 0.2846 3.077

The simulation using the latent formulation of the model is implemented in the sim_ord_latent() function. We define the dataset dat with predictors. Then the model formula is specified within the function as location = ~along with the vector of regression coefficients (beta), baseline probabilities (prob0), and the link function. The function returns a dataset with the simulated 𝑌 and the latent variable (this is possible only because we simulated the data, otherwise 𝑌 ⋆ cannot be observed by definition). produces a meaningful visual representation of using a specific set of thresholds (see Figure 6). Thus with two groups for example, the thresholds are the 𝑘 probabilities of the ordinal variable 𝑌 for the reference group (when 𝑥 = 0).
[Figure 6 about here]

Regression coefficients. For probit models, we can set the 𝛽 𝑗 to be in standardized (i.e., Cohen's 𝑑-like) units. For a categorical variable as the previous example with the group, 𝛽 𝑗 is the degree of separation in standard deviation unit between the two latent distributions. For logit models, we can set the odds ratio. Meaningful odds ratios can be derived from previous literature, meta-analyses or converted from other effect sizes. For example, Sánchez-Meca, Marín-Martínez, and Chacón-Moscoso (2003) proposed some equations to convert between odds ratios and Cohen's 𝑑. A Cohen's 𝑑 = 0.5 is usually considered a plausible medium effect size and corresponds to an odds ratio of ≈ 2.47.

We can also calculate and plot the predicted probabilities (i.e., 𝑔 -1 (𝜂)) given the predictors and the chosen regression coefficients. In this way, we can try different values and see if predicted probabilities are plausible or not. The cat_latent_plot() and num_latent_plot() functions can be for respectively a categorical (Figures 7) and predictor. On the left the shift in the latent mean and on the right the impact on the expected probabilities. The plot can be created using cat_latent_plot(m = c(0, 1), s = 1, prob0 = rep(1/4, 4), link = "logit").
[Figure 8 about here]

div.head: 2x2 interaction
div.p: A common research design could be a 2x2 factorial design. In this example we have two main effects and the interaction. By default R uses dummy coding but setting sum-to-zero contrasts (e.g., 0.5 and -0.5) for a factorial design is convenient. In this way, 𝛽 1 will be the main effect of 𝑋 1 , 𝛽 2 the main effect of 𝑋 2 , and 𝛽 3 the interaction (thus the difference of differences). Equation ( 6) shows the model formula. 𝛽 1 = 1 is the regression coefficient. The plot can be created using num_latent_plot(x = runif(100), b1 = 1, prob0 = c(0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1), link = "probit") #> data: dat #> #> link threshold nobs logLik AIC niter max.grad cond.H #> probit flexible 400 -390.29 790.57 4(0) 2.20e-07 2.1e+01 #> #> Coefficients: #> Estimate Std. In this case, by doing alpha_to_prob(fit$alpha, link = "probit") we should recover the probs0 vector. x11 is the main effect thus the difference in 𝑧 scores between a and b averaging over x2. The same holds for x21. x11:x21 is the interaction thus difference of differences in 𝑧 scores (see Figure 9).

div.head: Numerical by categorical interaction
div.p: Another common scenario is the interaction between a numerical variable 𝑥 and a categorical variable 𝑔. For simplicity, we simulate the factor with two levels and the numerical variable sampled from a uniform distribution between 0 and 1. set.seed(2024) n <-100 k <-3 dat <-data.frame(x = runif(n), g = rep(c("a", "b"), each = n/2)) dat$g <-factor(dat$g) contrasts(dat$g) <-c(0.5, -0.5) probs0 <-rep(1/k, k) dat <-sim_ord_latent(~x * g, beta = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.5), prob0 = probs0, link = "probit", data = dat) fit <-clm(y ~x * g, data = dat, link = "probit") summary(fit)

Again, x is the slope of the numerical predictor averaging over g (given that g has been coded with sum-to-zero contrast) thus the increase in 𝑧 scores for a unit increase in x.
g1 is the main effect of the factor evaluated when 𝑥 = 0 (centering 𝑥 will change the parameter interpretation). The x:g1 is the difference between the slopes of the two groups.

div.head: Power Analysis
div.p: In this section, we introduce how to estimate the statistical power. Power analysis is a crucial and often necessary step when planning a confirmatory study (Lakens, 2022) or preparing a pre-registration or registered report (Chambers & Tzavella, 2022). Furthermore, statistical power for complex models can only be estimated using Monte Carlo simulations.

Formally the power is defined as the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis 𝐻 0 . For simple cases (e.g., a t-test) the power can be calculated analytically while in complex cases simulating data is the best approach. We present a general example and categorical variables. The plot shows the predicted probabilities with 95% confidence intervals as a function of predictors. A similar plot can be produced using plot(ggeffects::ggpredict(fit, terms = c("x[all]", "g")))
that, as for the previous simulations, can be easily extended.
The general workflow for a power simulation can be summarized as:

1. Specify the research design, e.g., 2x2 factorial design 2. Specify the effect/parameter of interest, e.g., the interaction effect 3. Define the simulation conditions, e.g., a range of sample size, effect size, etc. Instead of calculating a single value, a more informative approach is plotting power curves. We repeat the previous simulation using different sample sizes.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this tutorial, we presented the CM model in terms of model fitting, parameters interpretation, and data simulation. The presented data simulation approach is really flexible and can be extended to scenarios beyond the examples above. Nowadays, data simulation is a crucial skill when planning studies especially when no analytical solution to power analysis is available. A potential limitation of the tutorial is that there are several plausible scenarios that we did not discuss. For example, the PO assumption can be relaxed fitting more complex models. Simulating models without the PO assumption is and the y axis the estimated power. The red dotted line highlights the 80% power level.

more challenging because they involve extra parameters. The simulation approach is still valid but requires a more complex setup. At the same time, often participants repond to multiple items creating a multilevel data structure with random intercepts and slopes. The supplementary materials (https://osf.io/93h5j) contain additional examples for mixed-effects models and how to simulate non-PO models.
